_comment: Per-chart narratives. CI (build_prompt.py -> GitHub Models -> write_narrative.py) overwrites these from live numbers; this committed copy is the fallback so the page always reads well. source = 'fallback' | 'github-models'.

notes.fossil: As of June 2026, WTI crude oil is priced at $84.38 per barrel, Brent crude at $86.99 per barrel, and US regular gasoline at $4.00 per gallon. Henry Hub natural gas is notably more volatile at $2.80 per MMBtu. Indexed to 2019 levels (set at 100), natural gas exhibited the largest price swings, peaking sharply in 2022 before retreating, whereas crude oil and gasoline prices moved more closely in tandem. This price volatility in natural gas reflects market sensitivity to supply and demand disruptions distinct from oil and gasoline dynamics.
notes.transition: Levelised cost of electricity, the average net cost to produce electricity over a plant’s lifetime, shows solar photovoltaic (PV) at $44/MWh and onshore wind at $33/MWh, both now cheaper than new coal ($110/MWh) or gas combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT) at $76/MWh. Offshore wind remains costlier at $75/MWh but close to gas. The roughly 90% decline in solar PV's levelised cost since 2010—from around $460/MWh to $44/MWh—illustrates the dramatic improvements in technology and economies of scale, greatly enhancing the competitiveness of renewable power generation.
notes.currency: An estimated 20% and rising share of global oil trade is now settled outside the US dollar, reflecting a gradual shift though the dollar remains dominant. This estimate, lacking official confirmation, is driven in part by Russia's pivot to Asian buyers and increasing use of yuan and rupee for settlement of cargoes. Despite this, the majority of oil trade continues to rely on the US dollar, underscoring its central role in global energy markets.
notes.now: Current fossil fuel prices show a divergence in volatility and dynamics among oil, gas, and gasoline, with natural gas standing out for its variability. Meanwhile, renewable electricity generation costs have fallen significantly, with solar and onshore wind now undercutting new coal and gas, signaling a competitive energy transition landscape. The oil market’s shifting currency base is gradual yet noteworthy, reflecting broader geopolitical and trade realignments within the global energy complex.
